question:
A 69-year-old man is brought to the emergency room by his daughter due to confusion. She reports that her father did not remember who she was yesterday, and his refrigerator was completely empty when she tried to make him lunch. She states that he was acting like himself when she visited him last week. She also notes that he has struggled with alcoholism for many years and has not seen a doctor in over two decades. She is unsure if he has any other chronic medical conditions. In the emergency room, the patient’s temperature is 101.2°F (38.4°C), pulse is 103/min, respirations are 22/min, and O2 saturation is 92% on room air. His BMI is 17.1 kg/m^2. Physical exam reveals an extremely thin and frail man who is not oriented to person, place, or time. As he is being examined, he becomes unresponsive and desaturates to 84%. He is intubated and admitted to the intensive care unit for what is found to be pneumonia, and the patient is started on total parental nutrition as he is sedated and has a history of aspiration from a prior hospitalization. Two days later, physical exam is notable for new peripheral edema. Laboratory tests at that time reveal the following:

Serum:
Na+: 133 mEq/L
Cl-: 101 mEq/L
K+: 2.4 mEq/L
HCO3-: 24 mEq/L
BUN: 22 mg/dL
Glucose: 124 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Phosphate: 1.1 mg/dL
Mg2+: 1.0 mg/dL

Which of the following could have prevented the complication seen in this patient?

options.opa: Slow initiation of total parenteral nutrition (TPN)

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Malnutrition -> Low BMI -> Increased risk of complications -> 70% CHAIN: Pneumonia -> Increased metabolic demands -> Worsening malnutrition -> 60% CHAIN: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) -> Risk of refeeding syndrome -> Electrolyte imbalances -> 80% CHAIN: Low BMI -> Increased risk of refeeding syndrome -> Electrolyte imbalances -> 70% CHAIN: Use of low-sugar TPN -> Reduced risk of refeeding syndrome -> Prevention of electrolyte imbalances -> 70%
enhanced_information: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) carries a risk of refeeding syndrome due to rapid nutrient reintroduction, leading to electrolyte imbalances. Low-sugar TPN may reduce this risk by preventing rapid shifts in electrolytes. Enteral nutrition could have been a safer option to prevent complications in this malnourished patient, avoiding the potential adverse effects of TPN.
analysis: The core medical principle here is the prevention of refeeding syndrome in a malnourished patient receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Refeeding syndrome can lead to electrolyte imbalances, which can manifest as peripheral edema and other complications. Enteral nutrition is generally considered a safer option in malnourished patients to prevent these complications. While low-sugar TPN may reduce the risk of electrolyte shifts, enteral nutrition remains the preferred choice in this scenario.
